passages.t: A peace offering from the herd
passages.happening:
“If one’s offering is a peace offering and he offers an animal from the herd, whether male or female, he must present it without blemish before the LORD” (verse 1).

The worshiper lays his hand on its head and kills it at the entrance to the tent. The priests sprinkle the blood on all sides of the altar (verse 2).

From the animal he brings the fat that covers the inner parts, both kidneys with their fat, and the lobe of the liver (verses 3-4). Aaron's sons burn these on the altar “as an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The burnt offering went up to God whole. The grain offering fed the priests. The peace offering is the one sacrifice an ordinary family ate. Later the book explains how it was shared: the fat went to God on the altar, the breast and the right thigh went to the priests, and the rest was a feast for the worshiper and his household (7:31-34).

Most people in ancient Israel did not eat meat every day. Flocks and herds were a family's wealth, kept for milk, wool and work. To kill an animal usually meant a festival, a guest or a celebration. The peace offering made such a meal an act of worship. A family ate it before the LORD, as people at peace with him.

The Hebrew name is shelamim. Most scholars link it with shalom, the word for peace, wholeness and well-being. Translations call it a peace offering, a fellowship offering or a sacrifice of well-being. Leviticus presents it less as a payment to get peace than as the celebration of people who already have it. The order of the book is worth noticing. The meal of peace with God is described before the offerings for sin.

The fat named here is the hard fat packed round the inner organs. It was thought the richest part of the animal, and Hebrew uses the word for fat to mean the best of anything. Giving it to God meant giving him the best share.

Unlike the burnt offering, this animal may be male or female. And no birds are listed.
passages.later:
When the covenant was sealed at Mount Sinai, young men “sacrificed young bulls as peace offerings to the LORD” (Exodus 24:5), and the leaders of Israel went up the mountain: “they saw Him, and they ate and drank” (Exodus 24:11).

Moses told Israel what such meals were for: “There, in the presence of the LORD your God, you and your households shall eat and rejoice” (Deuteronomy 12:7).

The New Testament does not tie Jesus to the peace offering by name, so the links are links of theme. Paul says of Christ, “For He Himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). And when he explains the Lord's Supper, he points to Israel's meals: “Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar?” (1 Corinthians 10:18).
passages.asks: The peace offering ended in a meal eaten before God by people at peace with him. Ask whether you think of God mostly as someone to satisfy, or as someone who wants you at his table. And ask whom you could invite to share a meal of thanks with you.

passages.happening:
“If, however, one’s peace offering to the LORD is from the flock, he must present a male or female without blemish” (verse 6).

If it is a lamb, he lays his hand on its head and kills it in front of the tent, and the priests sprinkle its blood on the altar (verses 7-8). He brings its fat, including “the entire fat tail cut off close to the backbone”, with the kidneys and the lobe of the liver (verses 9-10). “Then the priest is to burn them on the altar as food, an offering made by fire to the LORD” (verse 11).

If it is a goat, the steps are the same (verses 12-15). The priest burns the fat, and the passage ends: “All the fat is the LORD’s” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The chapter sets three paragraphs side by side: an animal from the herd, a lamb, a goat. Each follows the same steps. As in chapter 1, the repeating teaches something. The person with an ox and the person with a goat stand on the same footing before God.

One detail is new. The sheep of that land were of a fat-tailed breed, still raised in the Middle East, whose broad tail stores a heavy mass of fat. Cooks prized it. It goes to God with the rest of the fat.

Twice the burned portion is called ‘food’ (verses 11 and 16). Israel shared that word with its neighbors, whose temples set out daily meals before the statues of their gods. Israel kept the word but not the belief. There was no statue in the tent, and Israel's own songs say that God does not need feeding.

The liver's lobe is named each time. Diviners in the ancient world read the livers of sheep to learn the will of their gods, and clay models of livers used for this have been found in Mesopotamia and at Canaanite sites such as Hazor. Some scholars suggest that burning the lobe on the altar kept it from such use. The text gives no reason.

Then the summary: ‘All the fat is the LORD’s.’ The best part is his.
passages.later:
A psalm has God say, “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof” (Psalm 50:12).

The story of Samuel shows how this order could be twisted. The sons of Eli, priests at Shiloh, sent a servant to seize meat before God's share had been burned. When a worshiper objected, “The fat must be burned first; then you may take whatever you want”, the servant threatened to take it by force (1 Samuel 2:16). The writer's judgment is plain: “they were treating the LORD’s offering with contempt” (1 Samuel 2:17).
passages.asks: God's share came first, and it was the best share. Ask what God gets from you: the first of your time, money and attention, or whatever is left. And ask where, like Eli's sons, you have taken for yourself what should have gone to God or to others first.

passages.happening:
The chapter closes with a single rule, given for every household and every generation.

“This is a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live: You must not eat any fat or any blood” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends by stepping away from the altar and into every home. The rule holds ‘wherever you live’. Every ordinary meal was to carry a reminder that life, and the best of what life gives, belongs to God.

The two parts of the rule have different roots. The rule about blood is older than Sinai; it goes back to Noah. Leviticus later gives its reason: the life of a creature is in its blood, and God has given blood for atonement on the altar (17:11). The rule about fat marks the best part of the animals used for sacrifice as God's own share (7:23-25). It means the hard fat round the organs, not the fat that runs through the meat.

Jewish practice has kept both rules, removing the blood from meat and cutting away the forbidden fat.
passages.later:
After the flood God told Noah, “you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it” (Genesis 9:4).

In the book of Acts the leaders in Jerusalem asked Gentile believers “to abstain from food polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals, and from blood” (Acts 15:20).
passages.hard:
Does the ban on fat and blood still apply to Christians?

Christians have answered in more than one way. Many read the request of Acts 15 as suited to its setting. It let Jewish and Gentile believers share one table. They note Mark's comment on the teaching of Jesus, “(Thus all foods are clean.)” (Mark 7:19). On this reading Christians are free in what they eat. Some churches and Christian groups have gone on avoiding blood as a standing command. The note on Acts 15:12-21 sets out the readings, and these notes take no side.

Behind both readings stands the conviction this chapter teaches. Life is a gift from God, and it is not ours to treat lightly.
passages.asks: A rule for the altar became a rule for the kitchen. Ask what small, daily habit helps you remember that your life is God's gift. And ask whether you treat any life, your own or another's, more lightly than a gift should be treated.
